Data Appreciation · Week 4 · Title

Organising data: tidy tables in a spreadsheet

Tidy data has one row per thing observed and one column per thing measured — and then a spreadsheet can do the work.

Next Generation Genius · Year 1 · Foundation

Data Appreciation · Week 4 · Goals

By the end of today

  • Lay out data as a tidy table
  • Enter and format it in Google Sheets
  • Sort and filter it
Data Appreciation · Week 4 · Idea 1

Understand it

A spreadsheet can only help if the data is tidy:

  • one row per observation (one person, one sale, one day);
  • one column per variable, with a clear header;
  • one value per cell, no units typed in ("3", not "3 hrs" — put the unit in the header);
  • no merged cells and no totals in the middle of the data.

In Google Sheets: View → Freeze → 1 row keeps headers visible; Data → Sort range orders rows; Data → Create a filter shows only the rows you choose without deleting anything. Never sort just one column — it breaks every row apart.

Data Appreciation · Week 4 · Key words

Key words

Tidy data
one row per observation, one column per variable
Header
the top row naming each column
Filter
show only some rows without deleting the others
Data Appreciation · Week 4 · Practice

Now you do it

  1. Open your survey responses in Google Sheets
  2. Check: one row per person, one column per question
  3. Freeze the header, sort by one column, filter by another

Need a hand? Before you type, draw the table on paper: what is one row? what are the columns?

Done early? Use COUNTIF to count how many answered each option of one question.

Data Appreciation · Week 4 · Assessment

How you will be assessed

  • Why should you never sort only ONE column of a table?
  • Put the steps for turning survey responses into a chart in order.
  • Show your survey data as a tidy table in Google Sheets, frozen header, with one sort and one filter applied.

Your work is marked against the rubric, and you may be asked to explain your choices. Show your own thinking.
